title: Night Diving With Manta Rays in Kona (I Wasn't Ready)
creator: Marco Bellini
description:
Ten mantas, one very bright light, and a lot of screaming into my regulator.

Dive operator: we went out of Honokohau Harbor with a local crew, 2 tank trip, one dusk dive and the manta dive.
Camera: GoPro HERO13 in a Backscatter housing with two video lights.

Please never touch a manta. It strips the mucus layer that protects their skin.

sentences.t: Okay, it's about five thirty, the sun's going down, and we are about to do the one dive I've wanted to do since I was a kid.
Night diving with manta rays off the coast of Kona.
I'm not going to lie, I'm a little nervous, I've only done two night dives before and both were kind of a disaster.
So here's how this works, because it's actually really clever.
The boats anchor at a spot called Manta Village, and everyone drops down to the sandy bottom at about thirty feet.
Divers put their lights in the middle, pointing up, almost like a campfire.
The lights attract plankton, the plankton attracts the mantas, and the mantas come in to feed right over your head.
You don't chase them, you don't touch them, you just kneel in the sand and wait.
Alright, we're going in, see you down there.
Okay, I'm back on the boat and I genuinely cannot stop shaking, and it's not from the cold.
For the first fifteen minutes nothing happened, just a lot of plankton and a very confused moray eel.
And then this shape just came out of the dark.
It was easily twelve feet across, and it did a full backflip about two feet from my mask.
I screamed, I'm not proud of it, but you can hear it on the footage.
By the end there were maybe ten of them, looping over the lights, barrel rolling, mouths wide open.
The guide told us each one has a unique spot pattern on its belly, and they've identified more than three hundred individuals here.
One of them, a big female, has been coming to this spot for over thirty years.
Thirty years, that manta is older than me.
Before we head back to the harbor, this video is brought to you by the Tidewater Reef Trust.
Tidewater is a nonprofit that restores damaged coral reefs, and they pay local fishermen to grow and replant coral instead of fishing on the reef.
So far they've replanted over two hundred thousand coral fragments across Hawaii, Fiji and the Philippines.
Healthy reefs are where a lot of the plankton and the small fish come from, so without them, you don't get nights like tonight.
Twenty-five dollars plants ten corals, and they send you the GPS location and photos of your patch as it grows.
If you want to help, head to tidewaterreef dot org slash marco, the link is down below.
Thanks to the Tidewater Reef Trust for sponsoring this one.
Okay, a couple of tips if you want to do this yourself.
You don't need to be an advanced diver, but get a few dives in first so your buoyancy is solid.
If you're bouncing off the bottom, you kick up sand and nobody can see anything.
If you don't dive at all, there's a snorkel version where you float at the surface holding a light board, and honestly the mantas come just as close.
Bring a hood or a thicker suit, because sitting still for forty five minutes gets cold fast, even in Hawaii.
And please, please don't reach out and touch them.
Their skin has a protective coating, and touching it can make them sick.
Alright, the crew is pulling the anchor, I'm starving, and I think there's a poke bowl with my name on it back in town.
Next week we're doing a lava tube cave dive, which I'm told is even creepier.
If you liked this, you know what to do, and I'll see you in the next one.
